item.title: Time-over-threshold versus pulse-height energy reconstruction in a PbWO$_4$ calorimeter read out by SiPMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.24189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The time over threshold (ToT) can be measured with a comparator and a time-to-digital converter, avoiding the waveform digitizers normally used to read out calorimeter prototypes. We assess how much the energy resolution degrades when the pulse height (PH) is replaced by the ToT, using data collected in June 2024 at the CERN PS T9 beam line with 2-6 GeV electrons on OREO, a calorimeter of two $3\times3$ matrices of PbWO$_4$ crystals read out by SiPMs and sampled at 500 MS/s, and 1-6 GeV electrons on a lead-glass calorimeter sampled at 100 MS/s. The ToT is emulated offline on the recorded waveforms and converted into an amplitude, so that the same reconstruction chain is applied to both estimators. For OREO in random orientation the PH gives $\sigma/\mu$ = 3.6% at 2 GeV and 2.4% at 6 GeV. A single-threshold ToT worsens the resolution by 50-80%, because one threshold cannot cover the dynamic range, while a dual-threshold ToT gives 3.9% and 2.6%, i.e. 6-10% worse than the PH. Extending the waveforms beyond the 1 $\mu$s acquisition window shows that the window is not the limiting factor, and an emulated shaper that reduces the decay time to 50-100 ns preserves the result with a ToT of 0.3-0.5 $\mu$s instead of 1.2 $\mu$s. The ToT-to-amplitude conversion can also be calibrated with a scan of the two thresholds, without any digitizer, with a resolution comparable to the one obtained with PH-based curves. For the lead glass, whose pulses are less than two samples wide at half maximum, the ToT cannot be emulated reliably. We also find that a previous analysis of the same data is consistent with a drift normalization that does not subtract the pedestals; subtracting them improves the resolution by up to 1.6 percentage points.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Carsi, Erik Vallazza

item.title: Development of microwave multiplexed readout for athermal phonon TES-based detectors
item.description: arXiv:2610.24300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continued advancements in sub-eV calorimetric measurements are being enabled through the athermal phonon detection channel, with applications spanning a diverse array of fields, including low-mass dark matter searches, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, and quantum information science. While Transition Edge Sensors (TESs) have achieved the lowest thresholds to date, they face significant scalability bottlenecks due to the inherent constraints of conventional SQUID readout architectures. To address this limitation, we present an update on R&D to develop practical, highly multiplexed, microwave readout for athermal phonon TESs, which can enable a dramatic increase in both sensor count and target mass, with a focus on sub-GeV dark matter searches as a target application. This work leverages advances from highly scaled mm-wave, x-ray, and gamma-ray TES systems, adapting them to the unique needs of low-threshold rare event measurements. We quantify the basic readout functionality and noise level in our dilution refrigerator testbed and demonstrate operation of a variety of TES devices with saturation powers significantly lower than mm-wave and x-ray devices. We demonstrate proof-of-concept multiplexed readout of background event pulses, bound the readout's contribution to the parasitic TES background load to <1 fW, and discuss a cryogenic inline RF filtering scheme. These results demonstrate practical solutions to several of the key challenges that must be solved before a next-generation athermal phonon detector at scale is realized.

item.title: Phonon-dominated thermal conductivity of a superconducting amorphous MoSi thin film
item.description: arXiv:2610.26136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use the differential 3{\omega} method to directly measure the temperature dependent thermal conductivity for about 90 nm Mo0.78Si0.22 thin films. The measurements are performed in a closed-cycle cryostat to access the temperature range between 50 K and 300 K. The MoSi thin films are capped with Al2O3 and probed with a Pt wire. The results show that the thermal conductivity does not satisfy the Wiedemann-Franz law. This implies that thermal transport in MoSi is not dominated by electrons but by phonon-like excitations, contrary to what is assumed in many electro-thermal models of superconducting devices. We argue that this property might be related to the weak localization visible in the resistivity as a function of temperature curves of the superconductor.
item.dc:creator: Jacopo Piantanida Chiesa, Tom Q. Post, Martin P. van Exter, Michiel J. A. de Dood

item.title: The RUBIK satellite payload concept: a 3D-segmented plastic scintillation-based particle tracking detector
item.description: arXiv:2610.26159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the design concept and first experimental results of RUBIK, a three-dimensional resolving plastic scintillation detector developed as a scientific payload for the Research and Observation in Medium Earth Orbit satellite mission of the Institute of Space Systems of the University of Stuttgart. The name RUBIK is inspired by the Rubik's Cube, a familiar example of a three-dimensional segmented structure, reflecting the 5x5x5 modular arrangement of the sensitive volume. The sensitive volume consists of 125 PVT-based plastic scintillator unit cubes, each penetrated by two perpendicularly aligned wavelength-shifting fibres, which guide scintillation photons to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), providing 50 independent readout channels. Custom readout electronics, comprising two discriminator boards with per-channel programmable thresholds, an FPGA-based data-acquisition board, and a dedicated power and bias distribution board, have been developed exclusively from commercial off-the-shelf components. A single-layer prototype with ten readout channels was used for concept validation through SiPM bias voltage and temperature characterisation, and a time-over-threshold based amplitude reconstruction method was validated against radioactive source and cosmic ray measurements. First hit-pattern measurements with 220 MeV protons at a clinical proton therapy facility confirmed that spatially resolved hit clusters consistent with the expected beam geometry were observable in the single-layer readout, demonstrating the capability to resolve particle-induced signal patterns as a first step towards 3D track reconstruction in the full instrument.

item.title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.26172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.

item.title: Characterization of the R14374-10 photomultiplier tube for the Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.26299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) is a planned cubic-kilometer-scale neutrino telescope that will be deployed in the Pacific Ocean, leveraging deep-sea infrastructure operated by Ocean Networks Canada (ONC). The first detector line will deploy 320 3-inch Hamamatsu R14374-10 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) to detect Cherenkov light produced by charged particles propagating through water, as well as light from calibration sources and optical backgrounds. This article presents the systematic characterization of all PMTs to be integrated into the first detector line prior to deployment, ensuring compliance with all detector acceptance criteria. All PMTs satisfy the specified performance criteria: the average transit-time spread (TTS) was measured to be $1.73\pm 0.15\,$ns, and the average charge resolution at a gain of \num{5e6} was $0.43\pm 0.03\,$pC; the average after-pulse rate was measured to be around 6$\,\%$. The integrated P-ONE data acquisition (DAQ) system was also tested and cross-validated against a laboratory digitization system. The second part of the paper presents an in-depth characterization of a subset of six PMTs, focusing on the key properties required for detector simulations, including linearity, after-pulse rate, quantum efficiency, and relative collection efficiency. PMT linearity was measured at a gain of \num{5e6} using the complete P-ONE readout electronics, and the response was found to remain linear for signals up to 150 photoelectrons. After-pulse contributions from $\text{Cs}^{+}$, $\text{He}^{+}$, and other ions were identified in the subset. The peak quantum efficiency was measured to be $27.0\pm0.7\,\%$ at 395\,nm. Using measurements of the relative detection efficiency, the collection efficiency was found to differ by a wavelength-independent offset of 10--15$\%$ across the measured wavelength range.

item.title: Optical imaging in dual-phase xenon time projection chambers for neutrinoless double beta decay searches
item.description:
arXiv:2610.26739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dual-phase xenon time projection chambers (TPCs) are the leading technology for WIMP dark matter searches and have also demonstrated competitive sensitivities to neutrinoless double beta decays (0$
u eta eta$) of \ce{^{136}Xe}. However, the large energy disparity between these two signals requires different detector optimizations. In particular, 0$
u eta eta$\ searches in liquid xenon desire efficient rejection of closely located multiscatters of background gamma rays near the 0$
u eta eta$\ energy, a capability achieved only in the vertical dimension in existing dual-phase xenon TPCs. We propose a highly customized, wide-angle optical system that can be conveniently integrated into large xenon TPCs and provide mm-scale transverse position resolution for MeV signals by imaging gas electroluminescence light. This approach preserves a TPC's low-energy sensitivity and optimizes a single experiment for both dark matter and 0$
u eta eta$\ searches. This paper discusses the design, simulated performance, and implications of the imaging system for future liquid xenon-based 0$
u eta eta$\ searches.
item.dc:creator: Adam D. Tidball, Jingke Xu, Brian G. Lenardo, Nicholas Antipa

item.title: Junction Geometry Survives an Unidentifiable Blur
item.description: arXiv:2610.23912v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Thin filaments cross in microscopy, and dispersed spectra cross on X-ray detectors. At a junction, where these structures cross or branch, how many straight arms meet, and which way do they go? Unknown blur obscures the answer. At a balanced crossing, distinct Gaussian blurs can even produce the same observation law. We show that the arms can still be recovered. For separated rays of nonvanishing weight and an unknown centered Gaussian-mixture blur, a distance combining arm count, directions, relative weights and supporting lines is bounded by a constant times the Euclidean difference in cell probabilities on a sufficiently fine fixed grid. The bound is uniform over a bounded model class, including unidentifiable blurs. From $n$ positions or photon counts, the minimax error is of order $n^{-1/2}$. This rate is proved for a global estimator. In practice we fit rays and blur by constrained local likelihood, reducing the BIC count when two detectors agree on fewer arms in the microscopy studies. Across three studies with protocols fixed before evaluation, on 360 crossings and branches assembled from measured single-molecule localizations, the fit gets the arm count and every direction within $10^\circ$ 24 to 37 percentage points more often than a tuned fixed-scale Hessian ridge detector, averaged over 25 to 400 localizations. On acute angles with correct counts, mean absolute error is $3.5^\circ$ to $4.3^\circ$, versus $10.4^\circ$ to $15.5^\circ$. On Chandra spectra, 38 of 90 fits at 800 photons find all four arms within $10^\circ$; among these, median error is $0.023^\circ$.

item.title: Missing Light, Misleading Confidence: Optical-Module Readout Loss and Signal Reliability in Neutrino Telescopes
item.description: arXiv:2610.24003v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical neutrino telescopes reduce the photomultiplier signals of an optical module or string segment to compact multichannel summaries, and readout loss can make these summaries unreliable. We asked whether availability-based quality gates, which accept a summary when enough of the readout was live, can certify a summary of inter-channel statistical consistency (called coherence here; not optical coherence) under readout loss, and where they fail. We used public IceCube pulses (9,484 string records) and the released hits of KM3NeT event KM3-230213A with controlled readout loss, together with a replay of real KM3NeT readout flags. In a two-by-two design we compared a published recursive support state with direct mask support, and calibrated every threshold on development records. The support state is a function of the mask and added no information. On IceCube the support-gated rule retained 0.16 percentage points more usable summaries, an effect of the window at which support was read that reversed sign at a looser tolerance; on KM3NeT it accepted nothing. The gates accepted only records with nearly intact masks, including records whose charge had been depleted by signal-dependent loss that the mask does not record. Pulse loss during live acquisition and timing jitter passed every availability gate, which then accepted summaries of which up to 66% were unreliable. Availability flags are therefore necessary but not sufficient, and signal-based checks are needed. This work uses public data and is not an IceCube or KM3NeT Collaboration result.
item.dc:creator: Thammarat Yawisit, Pittaya Pannil

item.title: PRIMA prototype spaceflight KID readout electronics laboratory characterization
item.description: arXiv:2610.24337v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present further development and testing of prototype kinetic inductance detector (KID) readout electronics for the PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA). PRIMA is a NASA Probe-class astrophysics mission concept with two science instruments, FIRESS and PRIMAger, which provide spectroscopic and polarimetric imaging from 24 to 261 um. Together these instruments will explore the far-infrared sky with spatial-spectral mapping speeds that exceed previous studies by orders of magnitude, opening a vast discovery space. This increase in mapping speed is achieved by densely packed ultra-sensitive KIDs and cryogenically cooled optics. The PRIMA flight readout electronics will use the build-to-print SpaceCube Mini v3.0 which houses a radiation-tolerant Kintex KU060 field programmable gate array (FPGA). A custom high-speed digitizer board is being designed along with an RF electronics (RFE) board. The RFE was designed to provide programmable gain, band filtering, and RF switching between instruments. The prototype readout electronics, including the RFE, use functionally equivalent parts to the flight parts. In this proceeding we measure the readout loopback noise performance in the second Nyquist zone and timestream cross-talk performance. We present preliminary sweeps with the prototype readout coupled to prototype FIRESS detectors. Lastly, we demonstrate a cosmic ray pulse detection and real-time removal with an algorithm implemented in firmware.

item.title: A 4-20 GHz Superconducting 90deg Hybrid Using Capacitively Loaded Coupled Lines for 2SB Heterodyne Receivers
item.description: arXiv:2610.24859v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We report the design and cryogenic characterisation of a broadband superconducting 90deg intermediate-frequency (IF) hybrid covering 4 to 20 GHz for sideband-separating (2SB) heterodyne receivers. The hybrid is implemented in thin-film niobium using capacitively loaded edge coupled transmission lines, avoiding the air-bridge interconnections required in Lange-coupler layouts while retaining a compact superconducting implementation with low loss and good quadrature balance. Cryogenic measurements using Vector Network Analyser (VNA) show amplitude and phase imbalance better than 0.6 dB and 6deg, respectively, across the full band. When used in a 2SB receiver, this level of IF balance is consistent with the observed image-rejection performance in the 10-20 dB range, for the full receiver. The design supports the development of wide-instantaneous-bandwidth 2SB receivers for millimeter and submillimeter observatories, improving spectral grasp for broadband line surveys and high-redshift line searches.

item.title: Correlated detection of electrons and ions emitted from laser-induced nanoplasmas in doped helium nanodroplets in the single-shot single-cluster regime
item.description: arXiv:2610.26280v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present single-cluster single-shot correlated measurements of electron velocity-map images and ion time-of-flight traces from individual laser-induced nanoplasmas in xenon-doped helium nanodroplets. Simultaneous detection associates the ion composition, ion kinetic energies, and electron energies with the same nanoplasma event. The detected ion composition separates events into populations dominated by He+ mono-cations versus those dominated by He^{2+} di-cations, with markedly different ion energies and electron kinetic energies. The He+-dominated population correlates well with low electron kinetic energies (< 0.5 eV), whereas the distribution of maximum electron kinetic energies for the He^{2+}-dominated population shows a peak around 1 eV. Molecular dynamics simulations averaged over the focal volume suggest that local laser intensity contributes to this separation. These correlations provide single-event observables for classifying nanoplasmas and will support real-time shot-to-shot sorting in single-particle coherent diffractive imaging experiments.
item.dc:creator: Keshav Sishodia, Cristian Medina, Robert Moshammer, Thomas Pfeifer, Andreas Heidenreich, Marcel Mudrich, Sivarama Krishnan

item.title: Optical effects in Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs)
item.description: arXiv:2604.27399v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optical time projection chambers (OTPCs) are well suited for applications that require the highest spatial resolution for particle track reconstruction. The MIGDAL experiment uses a glass GEM-based OTPC and observes a systematic excess in both the intensity and width of particle tracks in its optical readout, when compared with charge readout simulations. One hypothesis is that scintillation light produced inside a GEM hole during the avalanche propagates through the GEM substrate and exits neighboring holes. We present lab measurements testing this hypothesized optical broadening effect in three types of GEM substrates: glass, ceramic, and FR4. Our observations quantify this optical broadening and demonstrate it to be strongest in glass GEMs. Additionally, we use Geant4 simulations to both reproduce our observations and quantify optical broadening effects in realistic charge avalanches. Applying our glass GEM effects to simulated particle tracks yields increases of track intensity and widths by up to approximately 26% and 31%, respectively. This may explain the larger-than-expected track intensities and widths observed in the MIGDAL OTPC. This effect may be relevant to GEM-based OTPCs, with its magnitude depending on the GEM structure and detector-specific optical configuration.
item.dc:creator: D. Edgeman, F. M. Brunbauer, M. Gardner, D. Loomba, P. A. Majewski, T. Marley, L. Millins, T. Neep, K. Nikolopoulos, J. Schueler, E. Tilly, W. Thompson

item.title: Time performance of USTC-IME LGAD under synchrotron light source focused X-ray
item.description: arXiv:2609.00972v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The time performance of Low Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs), designed by the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) and fabricated by the Institute of Microelectronics of Chinese Academy of Sciences (IME), was characterized at the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). The experiment was conducted at the BL16B1 beamline, which delivers a focused X-ray beam with a diameter of 500 \textmu\text{m}, a repetition period of 2 ns, and a photon energy of 10 keV. Using a fast oscilloscope, waveforms containing continuous signal pulses were recorded within a 50 ns time window. The LGAD under test successfully resolved the 2 ns period of the SSRF. To mitigate pile-up effects and extract pulse-by-pulse information from the acquired waveforms, a waveform-level global template fitting method was employed. The time resolution was then estimated using a combined profile likelihood approach, with a restricted maximum-likelihood (REML) correction accounting for the per-waveform degrees of freedom, yielding a value of 136.8 $\pm$ 0.15 (stat.) $\pm$ 11.9 (syst.) ps. The complete reconstruction and fitting chain was validated end-to-end using simulated waveforms in which the timing deviations of individual large pulses were drawn from Gaussian distributions with fixed standard deviations. The effect of random photon absorption depth on the time resolution of LGADs was studied through dedicated simulations.
item.dc:creator: Tianao Wang, De Zhang, Zheng Liang, Chaozhi Li, Jiaqi Luo, Yu Nie, Tianshuo Yue, Zebo Tang, Hao Liang, Tongpu Yu, Wanbing He, Yanwen Liu

item.title: SynradG4: A Geant4-Based Extension for Synchrotron Radiation Background Studies in the ePIC Detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
item.description: arXiv:2408.11709v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will operate at high luminosity with multi-GeV, high-current electron beams, resulting in substantial synchrotron radiation (SR) emission in the electron storage ring (ESR). A detailed understanding of SR photon transport in the complex three-dimensional interaction region (IR) geometry is critical for estimating backgrounds in the ePIC detector and for developing effective shielding and masking strategies. This paper presents SynradG4, an EIC-specific extension of Geant4 for fast photon tracking in vacuum based on established models of SR reflection and rough-surface scattering. SynradG4 integrates the specular and diffuse photon reflection models of Synrad+ into the Geant4 geometry and field framework, while disabling all bulk matter interactions to achieve high-statistics transport through the 50-m-long IR vacuum system. The absorbed photons are then passed to a second-stage DD4hep simulation, in which electromagnetic processes such as photoabsorption, Compton scattering, Rayleigh scattering, and fluorescence are enabled for their propagation through the beam pipe and detector materials. SynradG4 is not intended to replace general SR simulation codes; rather, it complements them by providing the workflow and geometry integration capabilities needed for EIC-specific background studies. Benchmark tests show that SynradG4 reproduces Synrad+ to within about 1% for both specular and diffuse reflection, and that it agrees well with Synrad3D and with the native Geant4 X-ray reflection model for smooth surfaces. Using the full IR geometry and machine lattice, we present the first SR background estimates for the ePIC detector and evaluate the impact of potential SR masks.
item.dc:creator: Andrii Natochii

item.title: An Algebra Bundle for Non-Composable Coincidence Probabilities in Gamma-ray Spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2512.00095v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding nuclear level schemes from the detection of emitted gamma-rays is, at its core, a combinatorial problem. The transition matrix formalism that treats nuclear decay as a Markov process is a well established treatment for the prediction of emitted and detected gamma-rays. However, with the path algebra being the underlying algebra of such matrix methods, the formalism is restricted to calculating probabilities only for composable paths through the decay. This paper presents a new algebra that allows for the calculations of non-composable coincidence probabilities offering a more complete formalism for the prediction of gamma-ray spectra. The aim of this \textit{coincidence algebra} is to provide a general treatment for predicting all full energy summing peaks for composable and non-composable transitions. Non-composable summing peaks often corrupt peaks of interest by creating doublets in the energy spectra. The coincidence algebra serves as a tool for investigating any possible doublets produced from full energy coincidence summing. This formalism is tested for the prediction of gamma-ray peaks in the electron capture of $^{133}$Ba and compared to the results a Geant4 simulation of the decay within the GRIFFIN spectrometer. It is also shown how the path algebra formalism may be useful for understanding uncertainty propagation in nuclear level schemes.
item.dc:creator: Liam L. Schmidt

item.title: Optomechanical Detection of Individual Gas Collisions
item.description: arXiv:2604.18371v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate the detection of momentum transfers from individual collisions of Kr, Xe, and SF$_6$ with an optically levitated nanoparticle, finding good agreement with theoretical expectations. The observed event rates accurately measure the gas partial pressures, while the spectral shape provides a sensitive probe of the surface properties of the nanoparticle, including its temperature. The reconstruction of impulse signals as small as 200 keV/$c$ further establishes that levitated optomechanical sensors can reach the sensitivity required for precision measurements of fundamental particle interactions, and demonstrates a proof-of-principle for a primary pressure sensor based on the detection of individual gas particle collisions.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Han Tseng, Clarke A. Hardy, T. W. Penny, Cecily Lowe, Jacqueline Baeza-Rubio, Daniel Carney, David C. Moore

item.title: Accounting for the detection response brings cavity ring-down spectroscopy to sub-permille accuracy
item.description: arXiv:2609.04027v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For nearly four decades, cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS) has been among the simplest, most widely used absorption techniques, requiring no calibration because it measures decay times, not intensities. Yet as accuracy requirements have tightened, CRDS has proven strikingly inconsistent: reported errors range from several percent to the permille level - the signature of an uncontrolled systematic effect so far worked around rather than resolved. This has confined applications demanding the highest accuracy - from testing ab initio theory to atmospheric sensing and quantum-based metrology - to a handful of laboratories relying on advanced calibration or architectures, at the cost of simplicity. Here we show the main source was hiding in plain sight: the detection chain's transient response. It distorts every ring-down, biasing the retrieved decay times differently from instrument to instrument - a bias that routine truncation of the early decay masks rather than removes. We measure this response with a calibration-free beat-note method and build it into the ring-down model. Validation uses a well-characterized carbon monoxide transition and an independent frequency-based reference. Across four detection configurations, line-intensity biases of up to 14 % shrink 41- to 87-fold, the results converge, reaching up to sub-permille agreement with the reference. This holds down to 4 us ring-down times, extending accurate CRDS to stronger absorption. Independent of the absorbing species and requiring no change to the CRDS setup, the approach turns a technique valued for its simplicity into one equally valued for its accuracy. Benchmark-quality measurement thus comes within reach of any CRDS laboratory.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Chell, Marcin Gibas, Szymon W\'ojtewicz, Jakub {\L}asocha, Daniel Lisak, Agata Cygan
